passages.text: Euelpides: Do you think I should walk straight for yon tree?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Cursed beast, what are you croaking to me? . . . to retrace my steps?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Why, you wretch, we are wandering at random, we are exerting ourselves only to return to the same spot; we're wasting our time.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: To think that I should trust to this crow, which has made me cover more than a thousand furlongs!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: And that I, in obedience to this jay, should have worn my toes down to the nails!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: If only I knew where we were . . .
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Could you find your country again from here?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: No, I feel quite sure I could not, any more than could Execestides find his.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Alas!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Aye, aye, my friend, it's surely the road of alases we are following.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: That Philocrates, the bird-seller, played us a scurvy trick,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: when he pretended these two guides could help us to find Tereus, the Epops, who is a bird, without being born of one. He has indeed sold us this jay, a true son of Tharrhelides, for an obolus, and this crow for three, but what can they do? Why, nothing whatever but bite and scratch!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: What's the matter with you then, that you keep opening your beak? Do you want us to fling ourselves headlong down these rocks? There is no road that way.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Not even the vestige of a trail in any direction
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: And what does the crow say about the road to follow?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: By Zeus, it no longer croaks the same thing it did.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: And which way does it tell us to go now?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: It says that, by dint of gnawing, it will devour my fingers.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: What misfortune is ours! we strain every nerve to get to the crows, do everything we can to that end, and we cannot find our way!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Yes, spectators, our madness is quite different from that of Sacas. He is not a citizen, and would fain be one at any cost; we, on the contrary, born of an honorable tribe and family and living in the midst of our fellow-citizens,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: we have fled from our country as hard as ever we could go. It's not that we hate it; we recognize it to be great and rich, likewise that everyone has the right to ruin himself paying taxes; but the crickets only chirrup among the fig-trees for a month or two,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: whereas the Athenians spend their whole lives in chanting forth judgments from their law-courts. That is why we started off with a basket, a stew-pot and some myrtle boughs and have come to seek a quiet country
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: in which to settle. We are going to Tereus, the Epops, to learn from him, whether, in his aerial flights, he has noticed some town of this kind.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Here! look!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: What's the matter?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Why, the crow has been directing me
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: to something up there for some time now.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: And the jay is also opening it beak and craning its neck to show me I know not what. Clearly, there are some birds about here. We shall soon know, if we kick up a noise to start them.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Do you know what to do? Knock your leg against this rock.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: And you your head to double the noise.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Well then use a stone instead; take one and hammer with it.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Good idea! He does so. Ho there, within! Slave! slave!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: What's that, friend! You say, slave, to summon Epops? It would be much better to shout, Epops, Epops!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Well then, Epops! Must I knock again? Epops!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Trochilus: Rushing out of a thicket. Who's there? Who calls my master?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Apollo the Deliverer! what an enormous beak!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Trochilus: Good god! they are bird-catchers.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: But is it so terrible? Wouldn't it be better to explain things?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Trochilus: You're done for.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: But we are not men.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Trochilus: What are you, then?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: I am the Fearling, an African bird.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Trochilus: You talk nonsense.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Well, then, just ask it of my feet.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Trochilus: And this other one, what bird is it? To Pisthetaerus. Speak up!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: I? I am a Crapple, from the land of the pheasants.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: But you yourself, in the name of the gods! what animal are you?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Trochilus: Why, I am a slave-bird.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Why, have you been conquered by a cock?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Trochilus: No, but when my master was turned into a hoopoe, he begged me to become a bird also, to follow and to serve him.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Does a bird need a servant, then?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Trochilus: That's no doubt because he was once a man. At times he wants to eat a dish of sardines from Phalerum; I seize my dish and fly to fetch him some. Again he wants some pea-soup; I seize a ladle and a pot and run to get it.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: This is, then,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: truly a running-bird. Come, Trochilus, do us the kindness to call your master.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Trochilus: Why, he has just fallen asleep after a feed of myrtle-berries and a few grubs.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Never mind; wake him up.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Trochilus: I am certain he will be angry. However, I will wake him to please you.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: You cursed brute! why, I am almost dead with terror!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Oh! my god! it was sheer fear that made me lose my jay.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Ah! you big coward! were you so frightened that you let go your jay?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: And did you not lose your crow, when you fell sprawling on the ground? Tell me that.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Not at all.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Where is it, then?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: It flew away.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: And you did not let it go? Oh! you brave fellow!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Open the thicket, that I may go out!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: By Heracles! what a creature! what plumage! What means this triple crest?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Who wants me?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: The twelve great gods have used you ill, it seems.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Are you twitting me about my feathers? I have been a man, strangers.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: It's not you we are jeering at.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: At what, then?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Why, it's your beak that looks so ridiculous to us.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: This is how Sophocles outrages me in his tragedies. Know, I once was Tereus.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: You were Tereus, and what are you now? a bird or a peacock?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: I am a bird.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Then where are your feathers? I don't see any.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: They have fallen off.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Through illness?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: No. All birds moult their feathers, you know, every winter, and others grow in their place. But tell me, who are you?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: We? We are mortals.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: From what country?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: From the land of the beautiful galleys.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Are you dicasts?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: No, if anything,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: we are anti-dicasts.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Is that kind of seed sown among you?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: You have to look hard to find even a little in our fields.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: What brings you here?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: We wish to pay you a visit.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: What for?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Because you formerly were a man, like we are,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: formerly you had debts, as we have, formerly you did not want to pay them, like ourselves; furthermore, being turned into a bird, you have when flying seen all lands and seas. Thus you have all human knowledge as well as that of birds.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: And hence we have come to you to beg you to direct us to some cosy town, in which one can repose as if on thick coverlets.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: And are you looking for a greater city than Athens ?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: No, not a greater, but one more pleasant to live in.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Then you are looking for an aristocratic country.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: I? Not at all! I hold the son of Scellias in horror.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: But, after all, what sort of city would please you best?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: A place where the following would be the most important business transacted. —Some friend would come knocking at the door quite early in the morning
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: saying, By Olympian Zeus, be at my house early, as soon as you have bathed, and bring your children too. I am giving a nuptial feast, so don't fail, or else don't cross my threshold when I am in distress.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Ah! that's what may be called being fond of hardships! To Pisthetaerus. And what say you?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: My tastes are similar.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: And they are?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: I want a town where the father of a handsome lad will stop in the street and say to me reproachfully as if I had failed him, Ah! Is this well done, Stilbonides?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: You met my son coming from the bath after the gymnasium and you neither spoke to him, nor kissed him, nor took him with you, nor ever once felt his balls. Would anyone call you an old friend of mine?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Ah! wag, I see you are fond of suffering. But there is a city of delights such as you want.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: It's on the Red Sea .
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Oh, no. Not a sea-port, where some fine morning the Salaminian galley can appear, bringing a process-server along. Have you no Greek town you can propose to us?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Why not choose Lepreum in Elis for your settlement?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: By Zeus! I could not look at Lepreum without disgust, because of Melanthius.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Then, again, there is the Opuntian Locris, where you could live.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: I would not be Opuntian for a talent.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: But come, what is it like to live with the birds? You should know pretty well.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Why, it's not a disagreeable life. In the first place, one has no purse.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: That does away with a lot of roguery.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: For food the gardens yield us white sesame,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: myrtle-berries, poppies and mint.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Why, 'tis the life of the newly-wed indeed.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Ha! I am beginning to see a great plan, which will transfer the supreme power to the birds, if you will but take my advice.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Take your advice? In what way?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: In what way? Well, firstly,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: do not fly in all directions with open beak; it is not dignified. Among us, when we see a thoughtless man, we ask, What sort of bird is this? and Teleas answers, It's a man who has no brain, a bird that has lost his head, a creature
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: you cannot catch, for it never remains in any one place.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: By Zeus himself! your jest hits the mark. What then is to be done?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Found a city.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: We birds? But what sort of city should we build?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Oh, really, really! you talk like such a fool!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Look down.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: I am looking.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Now look up.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: I am looking.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Turn your head round.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Ah! it will be pleasant for me if I end in twisting my neck off!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: What have you seen?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: The clouds and the sky.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Very well! is not this the pole of the birds then?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: How their pole?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Or, if you like it, their place. And since it turns and passes through the whole universe, it is called ‘pole.’ If you build and fortify it, you will turn your pole into a city.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: In this way you will reign over mankind as you do over the grasshoppers and you will cause the gods to die of rabid hunger.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: How so?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: The air is between earth and heaven. When we want to go to Delphi , we ask the Boeotians for leave of passage;
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: in the same way, when men sacrifice to the gods, unless the latter pay you tribute, you exercise the right of every nation towards strangers and don't allow the smoke of the sacrifices to pass through your city and territory.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: By earth! by snares! by network! by cages!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: I never heard of anything more cleverly conceived; and, if the other birds approve, I am going to build the city along with you.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Who will explain the matter to them?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: You must yourself. Before I came they were quite ignorant,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: but since I have lived with them I have taught them to speak.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: But how can they be gathered together?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Easily. I will hasten down to the thicket to waken my dear Procne
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: and as soon as they hear our voices, they will come to us hot wing.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: My dear bird, lose no time, please! Fly at once into the thicket and awaken Procne.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Chase off drowsy sleep, dear companion.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Let the sacred hymn gush from thy divine throat in melodious strains; roll forth in soft cadence your refreshing melodies to bewail the fate of Itys, which has been the cause of so many tears to us both.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Your pure notes rise through the thick leaves of the yew-tree right up to the throne of Zeus, where Phoebus listens to you, Phoebus with his golden hair. And his ivory lyre responds to your plaintive accents;
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: he gathers the choir of the gods and from their immortal lips pours forth a sacred chant of blessed voices.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Oh! by Zeus! what a throat that little bird possesses. He has filled the whole thicket with honey-sweet melody!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Hush!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: What's the matter?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Be still!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: What for?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Epops is going to sing again.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Epopopoi popoi popopopoi popoi, here, here, quick, quick, quick, my comrades in the air;
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: all you who pillage the fertile lands of the husbandmen, the numberless tribes who gather and devour the barley seeds, the swift flying race that sings so sweetly. And you whose gentle twitter
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: resounds through the fields with the little cry of tiotiotiotiotiotiotiotio; and you who hop about the branches of the ivy in the gardens;
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: the mountain birds, who feed on the wild olive-berries or the arbutus, hurry to come at my call, trioto, trioto, totobrix; you also, who snap up the sharp-stinging
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: gnats in the marshy vales, and you who dwell in the fine plain of Marathon, all damp with dew, and you, the francolin with speckled wings;
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: you too, the halcyons, who flit over the swelling waves of the sea, come hither to hear the tidings; let all the tribes of long-necked birds assemble here;
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: know that a clever old man has come to us, bringing an entirely new idea and proposing great reforms. Let all come to the debate here, here, here, here.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Torotorotorotorotix, kikkabau, kikkabau, torotorotorolililix.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Can you see any bird?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: By Phoebus, no! and yet I am straining my eyesight to scan the sky.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: It was hardly worth Epops' while to go and bury himself in the thicket like a hatching plover.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: A Bird: Torotix, torotix.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Wait, friend, there's a bird.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: By Zeus, it is a bird, but what kind? Isn't it a peacock?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Epops will tell us. What is this bird?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: It's not one of those you are used to seeing; it's a bird from the marshes.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Oh! oh! but he is very handsome with his wings as crimson as flame.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Undoubtedly; indeed he is called flamingo.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Hi! I say! You!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: What are you shouting for?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Why, here's another bird.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Aye, indeed; this one's a foreign bird too. To Epops. What is this bird from beyond the mountains with a look as solemn as it is stupid?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: He is called the Mede.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: The Mede! But, by Heracles, how, if a Mede, has he flown here without a camel?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Here's another bird with a crest.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Ah! that's curious. I say, Epops, you are not the only one of your kind then?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: This bird is the son of Philocles, who is the son of Epops; so that, you see, I am his grandfather; just as one might say, Hipponicus, the son of Callias, who is the son of Hipponicus.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Then this bird is Callias! Why, what a lot of his feathers he has lost!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: That's because he is honest; so the informers set upon him and the women too pluck out his feathers.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: By Poseidon, do you see that many-coloured bird? What is his name?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: This one? That's the glutton.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Is there another glutton besides Cleonymus?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: But why, if he is Cleonymus, has he not thrown away his crest?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: But what is the meaning of all these crests? Have these birds come to contend for the double stadium prize?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: They are like the Carians, who cling to the crests of their mountains for greater safety.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Oh, Poseidon! look what awful swarms of birds are gathering here!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: By Phoebus! what a cloud! The entrance to the stage is no longer visible so closely do they fly together.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Here is the partridge.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Why, there is the francolin.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: There is the poachard.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Here is the kingfisher.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: To Epops. What's that bird behind the kingfisher?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: That's the barber.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: What? a bird a barber?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Why, Sporgilus is one.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Here comes the owl.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: And who is it brings an owl to Athens ?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Here is the magpie, the turtle-dove, the swallow, the horned-owl, the buzzard, the pigeon, the falcon, the ring-dove, the cuckoo, the red-foot, the red-cap, the purple-cap, the kestrel, the diver, the ousel, the osprey, the woodpecker . . .
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Oh! what a lot of birds! Oh! what a lot of blackbirds! How they scold, how they come rushing up! What a noise! what a noise! Can they be bearing us ill-will? Oh! there! there! they are opening their beaks and staring at us.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Why, so they are.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: Popopopopopo. Where is he who called me? Where am I to find him?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: I have been waiting for you a long while! I never fail in my word to my friends.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: Tititititititi. What good news
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: have you for me?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Something that concerns our common safety, and that is just as pleasant as it is to the point. Two men, who are subtle reasoners, have come here to seek me.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: Where? How? What are you saying?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: I say, two old men have come from the abode of humans to propose a vast and splendid scheme to us.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: Oh! it's a horrible, unheard-of crime! What are you saying?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Never let my words scare you.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: What have you done to me?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: I have welcomed two men, who wish to live with us.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: And you have dared to do that!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Yes, and I am delighted at having done so.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: And are they already with us?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Just as much as I am.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Chorus: Ah! ah! we are betrayed; 'tis sacrilege! Our friend,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: he who picked up corn-seeds in the same plains as ourselves, has violated our ancient laws; he has broken the oaths that bind all birds; he has laid a snare for me, he has handed us over to the attacks of that impious race which, throughout all time,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: has never ceased to war against us.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: As for this traitorous bird, we will decide his case later, but the two old men shall be punished forthwith; we are going to tear them to pieces.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: It's all over with us.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: You are the sole cause of all our trouble.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Why did you bring me from down yonder?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: To have you with me.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Say rather to have me melt into tears.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Go on! you are talking nonsense. How will you weep with your eyes pecked out?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Chorus: Io! io! forward to the attack, throw yourselves upon the foe,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: spill his blood; take to your wings and surround them on all sides. Woe to them! let us get to work with our beaks, let us devour them.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Nothing can save them from our wrath, neither the mountain forests, nor the clouds that float in the sky, nor the foaming deep.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: Come, peck, tear to ribbons. Where is the chief of the cohort? Let him engage the right wing.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: This is the fatal moment. Where shall I fly to, unfortunate wretch that I am?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Wait! Stay here!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: That they may tear me to pieces?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: And how do you think to escape them?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: I don't know at all.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Come, I will tell you. We must stop and fight them. Let us arm ourselves with these stew-pots.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Why with the stew-pots?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: The owl will not attack us then.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: But do you see all those hooked claws?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Take the spit
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: and pierce the foe on your side.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: And how about my eyes?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Protect them with this dish or this vinegar-pot.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Oh! what cleverness! what inventive genius! You are a great general, even greater than Nicias, where stratagem is concerned.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: Forward, forward, charge with your beaks! Come, no delay.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Tear, pluck, strike, flay them, and first of all smash the stew-pot.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Oh, most cruel of all animals, why tear these two men to pieces, why kill them? What have they done to you? They belong to the same tribe, to the same family as my wife.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: Are wolves to be spared? Are they not our most mortal foes?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: So let us punish them.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: If they are your foes by nature, they are your friends in heart, and they come here to give you useful advice.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: Advice or a useful word from their lips, from them, the enemies of my forebears?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: The wise can often profit by the lessons of a foe, for caution is the mother of safety. It is just such a thing as one will not learn from a friend and which an enemy compels you to know. To begin with, it's the foe and not the friend that taught cities to build high walls, to equip long vessels of war;
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: and it's this knowledge that protects our children, our slaves and our wealth.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: Well then, I agree, let us first hear them, for that is best; one can even learn something in an enemy's school.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Their wrath seems to cool. Draw back a little.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: It's only justice, and you will thank me later.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: Never have we opposed your advice up to now.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: They are in a more peaceful mood; put down your stew-pot and your two dishes; spit in hand, doing duty for a spear, let us mount guard inside the camp
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: close to the pot and watch in our arsenal closely; for we must not fly.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: You are right. But where shall we be buried, if we die?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: In the Ceramicus; for, to get a public funeral, we shall tell the Strategi that we fell at Orneae, fighting the country's foes.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: Return to your ranks and lay down your courage beside your wrath as the hoplites do. Then let us ask these men who they are, whence they come,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: and with what intent. Here, Epops, answer me.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Are you calling me? What do you want of me?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: Who are they? From what country?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Strangers, who have come from Greece , the land of the wise.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: And what fate has led them hither to the land of the birds?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Their love for you and their wish to share your kind of life; to dwell and
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: remain with you always.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: Indeed, and what are their plans?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: They are wonderful, incredible, unheard of.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: Why, do they think to see some advantage that determines them to settle here? Are they hoping with our help
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: to triumph over their foes or to be useful to their friends?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: They speak of benefits so great it is impossible either to describe or conceive them; all shall be yours,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: all that we see here, there, above and below us; this they vouch for.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: Are they mad?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: They are the sanest people in the world.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: Clever men?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: The slyest of foxes, cleverness its very self, men of the world, cunning, the cream of knowing folk.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: Tell them to speak and speak quickly; why, as I listen to you, I am beside myself with delight.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Here, you there, take all these weapons and hang them up inside close to the fire, near the figure of the god who presides there and under his protection; To Pisthetaerus. as for you, address the birds, tell them why I have gathered them together.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Not I, by Apollo,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: unless they agree with me as the little ape of an armorer agreed with his wife, not to bite me, nor pull me by the balls, nor shove things into my . . .
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Do you mean this?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: No, I mean my eyes.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: Agreed.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Swear it.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: I swear it and, if I keep my promise, let judges and spectators give me the victory unanimously.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: It is a bargain.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: And if I break my word, may I succeed by one vote only.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Hearken, ye people! Hoplites, pick up your weapons and return to your firesides;
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: do not fail to read the decrees of dismissal we have posted.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Chorus: Man is a truly cunning creature, but nevertheless explain. Perhaps you are going to show me some good way
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: to extend my power, some way that I have not had the wit to find out and which you have discovered. Speak! 'tis to your own interest as well as to mine, for if you secure me some advantage, I will surely share it with you.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: But what object can have induced you to come among us? Speak boldly, for I shall not break the truce, —until you have told us all.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: I am bursting with desire to speak; I have already mixed the dough of my address and nothing prevents me from kneading it.... Slave! bring the chaplet and water, which you must pour over my hands. Be quick!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Is it a question of feasting? What does it all mean?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: By Zeus, no! but I am hunting for fine, tasty words to break down the hardness of their hearts. To the Chorus. I grieve so much for you, who at one time were kings...
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: We kings? Over whom?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: ... of all that exists, firstly of me and of this man, even of Zeus himself. Your race is older than Saturn, the Titans and the Earth.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: What, older than the Earth!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: By Phoebus, yes.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: By Zeus, but I never knew that before!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: That's because you are ignorant and heedless, and have never read your Aesop. He is the one who tells us that the lark was born before all other creatures, indeed before the Earth; his father died of sickness, but the Earth did not exist then; he remained unburied for five days, when the bird in its dilemma decided,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: for want of a better place, to entomb its father in its own head.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: So that the lark's father is buried at Cephalae.

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Hence, if they existed before the Earth, before the gods, the kingship belongs to them by right of priority.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Undoubtedly, but sharpen your beak well;
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Zeus won't be in a hurry to hand over his scepter to the woodpecker.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: It was not the gods, but the birds, who were formerly the masters and kings over men; of this I have a thousand proofs. First of all, I will point you to the cock, who governed the Persians before all other monarchs, before Darius and Megabazus.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: It's in memory of his reign that he is called the Persian bird.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: For this reason also, even to-day, he alone of all the birds wears his tiara straight on his head, like the Great King.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: He was so strong, so great, so feared, that even now, on account of his ancient power,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: everyone jumps out of bed as soon as ever he crows at daybreak. Blacksmiths, potters, tanners, shoemakers, bathmen, corn-dealers, lyre-makers and armorers, all put on their shoes and go to work before it is daylight.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: I can tell you something about that. It was the cock's fault that I lost a splendid tunic of Phrygian wool. I was at a feast in town, given to celebrate the birth of a child; I had drunk pretty freely
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: and had just fallen asleep, when a cock, I suppose in a greater hurry than the rest, began to crow. I thought it was dawn and set out for Halimus. I had hardly got beyond the walls, when a footpad struck me in the back with his bludgeon; down I went and wanted to shout, but he had already made off with my mantle.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: The Greeks?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage
