passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: When he called out cuckoo, all the Phoenicians hurried to the fields to reap their wheat and their barley.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Hence no doubt the proverb, Cuckoo! cuckoo! go to the fields, ye circumcised.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: So powerful were the birds that the kings of Grecian cities, Agamemnon, Menelaus, for instance,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: carried a bird on the tip of their scepters, who had his share of all presents.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: That I didn't know and was much astonished when I saw Priam come upon the stage in the tragedies with a bird, which kept watching Lysicrates to see if he got any present.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: But the strongest proof of all is that Zeus, who now reigns,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: is represented as standing with an eagle on his head as a symbol of his royalty; his daughter has an owl, and Phoebus, as his servant, has a hawk.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: By Demeter, the point is well taken. But what are all these birds doing in heaven?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: When anyone sacrifices and, according to the rite, offers the entrails to the gods, these birds take their share before Zeus.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Formerly men always swore by the birds and never by the gods. And even now Lampon swears by the goose whenever he wishes to deceive someone. Thus it is clear that you were once great and sacred,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: but now you are looked upon as slaves, as fools, as Maneses; stones
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: are thrown at you as at raving madmen, even in holy places. A crowd of bird-catchers sets snares, traps, limed twigs and nets of all sorts for you; you are caught, you are sold in heaps
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: and the buyers finger you over to be certain you are fat. Again, if they would but serve you up simply roasted; but they rasp cheese into a mixture of oil, vinegar and laserwort,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: to which another sweet and greasy sauce is added, and the whole is poured scalding hot over your back, for all the world as if you were diseased meat.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Chorus: Man, your words have
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: made my heart bleed; I have groaned over the treachery of our fathers, who knew not how to transmit to us the high rank they held from their forefathers. But 'tis a benevolent Genius, a happy Fate, that sends you to us;
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: you shall be our deliverer and I place the destiny of my little ones and my own in your hands with every confidence.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: But hasten to tell me what must be done; we should not be worthy to live, if we did not seek to regain our royalty by every possible means.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: First I advise that the birds gather together in one city and that they build a wall of great bricks, like that at Babylon , round the plains of the air and the whole region of space that divides earth from heaven.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Oh, Cebriones! oh, Porphyrion! what a terribly strong place!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Then, when this has been well done and completed, you demand back the empire from Zeus;
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: if he will not agree, if he refuses and does not at once confess himself beaten, you declare a sacred war against him and forbid the gods henceforward to pass through your country with their tools up, as hitherto, for the purpose of laying their Alcmenas, their Alopes, or their Semeles! if they try to pass through,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: you put rings on their tools so that they can't make love any longer. You send another messenger to mankind, who will proclaim to them that the birds are kings, that for the future they must first of all sacrifice to them, and only afterwards to the gods; that it is fitting to appoint to each deity the bird that has most in common with it.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: For instance, are they sacrificing to Aphrodite, let them at the same time offer barley to the coot; are they immolating a sheep to Poseidon, let them consecrate wheat in honor of the duck; if a steer is being offered to Heracles, let honey-cakes be dedicated to the gull; if a goat is being slain for King Zeus, there is a King-Bird, the wren, to whom the sacrifice of a male gnat is due before Zeus himself even.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: This notion of an immolated gnat delights me! And now let the great Zeus thunder!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: But how will mankind recognize us as gods and not as jays? Us, who have wings and fly?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: You talk rubbish! Hermes is a god and has wings and flies, and so do many other gods. First of all, Victory flies with golden wings, Eros is undoubtedly winged too,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: and Iris is compared by Homer to a timorous dove.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: But will not Zeus thunder and send his winged bolts against us?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: If men in their blindness do not recognize us as gods and so continue to worship the dwellers in Olympus ? Then a cloud of sparrows greedy for corn must descend upon their fields and eat up all their seeds;
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: we shall see then if Demeter will mete them out any wheat.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: By Zeus, she'll take good care she does not, and you will see her inventing a thousand excuses.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: The crows too will prove your divinity to them by pecking out the eyes of their flocks and of their draught-oxen; and then let Apollo cure them, since he is a physician and is paid for the purpose.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Oh! don't do that! Wait first until I have sold my two young bullocks.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: If on the other hand they recognize that you are God, the principle of life, that you are Earth, Kronos, Poseidon, they shall be loaded with benefits.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Name me one of these then.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Firstly, the locusts shall not eat up their vine-blossoms; a legion of owls and kestrels will devour them.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Moreover, the gnats and the gallbugs shall no longer ravage the figs; a flock of thrushes shall swallow the whole host down to the very last.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: And how shall we give wealth to mankind? This is their strongest passion.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: When they consult the omens, you will point them to the richest mines, you will reveal the paying ventures to the diviner,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: and not another shipwreck will happen or sailor perish.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: No more shall perish? How is that?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: When the auguries are examined before starting on a voyage, some bird will not fail to say, Don't start! there will be a storm, or else, Go! you will make a most profitable venture.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: I shall buy a trading-vessel and go to sea. I will not stay with you.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: You will discover treasures to them, which were buried in former times,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: for you know them. Do not all men say, None knows where my treasure lies, unless perchance it be some bird.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: I shall sell my boat and buy a spade to unearth the vessels.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: And how are we to give them health, which belongs to the gods?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: If they are happy, is not that the chief thing towards health?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: The miserable man is never well.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: Old Age also dwells in Olympus . How will they get at it? Must they die in early youth?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Why, the birds, by Zeus,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: will add three hundred years to their life.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: From whom will they take them?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: From whom? Why, from themselves. Don't you know the cawing crow lives five times as long as a man?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Ah! ah! these are far better kings for us than Zeus!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Far better, are they not? And firstly, we shall not have to build them temples of hewn stone, closed with gates of gold;
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: they will dwell amongst the bushes and in the thickets of green oak; the most venerated of birds will have no other temple than the foliage of the olive tree; we shall not go to Delphi or to Ammon
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: to sacrifice; but standing erect in the midst of arbutus and wild olives and holding forth our hands filled with wheat and barley, we shall pray them to admit us to a share of the blessings they enjoy
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: and shall at once obtain them for a few grains of wheat.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: Old man, whom I detested, you are now to me the dearest of all; never shall I, if I can help it, fail to follow your advice.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Chorus: Inspirited by your words,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: I threaten my rivals the gods, and I swear that if you march in alliance with me against the gods and are faithful to our just, loyal and sacred bond, we shall soon have shattered their scepter.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: We shall charge ourselves with the performance of everything that requires force; that which demands thought and deliberation shall be yours to supply.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: By Zeus! it's no longer
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: the time to delay and loiter like Nicias; let us act as promptly as possible.... In the first place, come, enter my nest built of brushwood and blades of straw, and tell me your names.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: That is soon done; my name is Pisthetaerus, and his,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides, of the deme Crioa.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Good! and good luck to you.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: We accept the omen.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Come in here.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Very well, you are the one who must lead us and introduce us.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Come then.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Oh! my god! do come back here. Hi! tell us how
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: we are to follow you. You can fly, but we cannot.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Well, well.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Remember Aesop's fables. It is told there that the fox fared very badly, because he had made an alliance with the eagle.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Be at ease. You shall eat a certain root
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: and wings will grow on your shoulders.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Then let us enter. Xanthias and Manodorus, pick up our baggage.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: Hi! Epops! do you hear me?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: What's the matter?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: Take them off to dine well and call your mate, the melodious Procne, whose songs are worthy of the Muses;
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: she will delight our leisure moments.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Oh! I conjure you, accede to their wish; for this delightful bird will leave her rushes at the sound of your voice;
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: for the sake of the gods, let her come here, so that we may contemplate the nightingale.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Let it be as you desire. Come forth, Procne, show yourself to these strangers.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Oh! great Zeus! what a beautiful little bird! what a dainty form! what brilliant plumage!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Do you know how dearly I should like to get between her thighs?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: She is dazzling all over with gold, like a young girl.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Oh! how I should like to kiss her!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Why, wretched man, she has two little sharp points on her beak!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: I would treat her like an egg, the shell of which we remove before eating it; I would take off her mask and then kiss her pretty face.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Let us go in.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Lead the way, and may success attend us. Epops goes into the thicket, followed by Pisthetaerus and Euelpides.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Chorus: Lovable golden bird, whom I cherish above all others, you, whom I associate with all my songs, nightingale,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: you have come, you have come, to show yourself to me and to charm me with your notes. Come, you, who play spring melodies upon the harmonious flute, lead off our anapests.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: Weak mortals, chained to the earth, creatures of clay as frail as the foliage of the woods, you unfortunate race, whose life is but darkness, as unreal as a shadow, the illusion of a dream, hearken to us, who are immortal beings, ethereal, ever young and occupied with eternal thoughts, for we shall teach you about all celestial matters;
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: you shall know thoroughly what is the nature of the birds, what the origin of the gods, of the rivers, of Erebus, and Chaos; thanks to us, even Prodicus will envy you your knowledge.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: At the beginning there was only Chaos, Night, dark Erebus, and deep Tartarus. Earth, the air and heaven had no existence.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Firstly, blackwinged Night laid a germless egg in the bosom of the infinite deeps of Erebus, and from this, after the revolution of long ages, sprang the graceful Eros with his glittering golden wings, swift as the whirlwinds of the tempest. He mated in deep Tartarus with dark Chaos, winged like himself, and thus hatched forth our race, which was the first to see the light.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: That of the Immortals did not exist until Eros had brought together all the ingredients of the world, and from their marriage Heaven, Ocean, Earth and the imperishable race of blessed gods sprang into being. Thus our origin is very much older than that of the dwellers in Olympus . We are the offspring of Eros; there are a thousand proofs to show it. We have wings and we lend assistance to lovers.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: How many handsome youths, who had sworn to remain insensible, have opened their thighs because of our power and have yielded themselves to their lovers when almost at the end of their youth, being led away by the gift of a quail, a waterfowl, a goose, or a cock.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Chorus: And what important services do not the birds render to mortals! First of all, they mark the seasons for them, springtime, winter, and autumn.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Does the screaming crane migrate to Libya , —it warns the husbandman to sow, the pilot to take his ease beside his tiller hung up in his dwelling, and Orestes to weave a tunic, so that the rigorous cold may not drive him any more to strip other folk. When the kite reappears, he tells of the return of spring and of the period when the fleece of the sheep must be clipped. Is the swallow in sight?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: All hasten to sell their warm tunic and to buy some light clothing. We are your Ammon, Delphi , Dodona , your Phoebus Apollo. Before undertaking anything, whether a business transaction, a marriage, or the purchase of food, you consult the birds by reading the omens, and you give this name of omen to all signs that tell of the future.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: With you a word is an omen, you call a sneeze an omen, a meeting an omen, an unknown sound an omen, a slave or an ass an omen. Is it not clear that we are a prophetic Apollo to you?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: If you recognize us as gods, we shall be your divining Muses, through us you will know the winds and the seasons, summer,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: winter, and the temperate months. We shall not withdraw ourselves to the highest clouds like Zeus, but shall be among you and shall give to you
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: and to your children and the children of your children, health and wealth, long life, peace, youth, laughter, songs and feasts; in short, you will all be so well off,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: that you will be weary and cloyed with enjoyment.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: First Semi-Chorus: Oh, rustic Muse of such varied note, tiotiotiotiotiotinx, I sing with you
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: in the groves and on the mountain tops, tiotiotiotinx. I poured forth sacred strains from my golden throat
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: in honor of the god Pan, tiotiotiotinx, from the top of the thickly leaved ash, and my voice mingles with the mighty choirs who extol Cybele on the mountain tops, totototototototototinx. 'Tis to our concerts that Phrynichus comes to pillage like a bee the ambrosia of his songs,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: the sweetness of which so charms the ear, tiotiotiotinx.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of First Semi-Chorus: If there is one of you spectators who wishes to spend the rest of his life quietly among the birds, let him come to us.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: All that is disgraceful and forbidden by law on earth is on the contrary honorable among us, the birds. For instance, among you it's a crime to beat your father, but with us it's an estimable deed; it's considered fine to run straight at your father and hit him, saying, Come, lift your spur if you want to fight.

passages.text: The runaway slave, whom you brand, is only a spotted francolin with us. Are you Phrygian like Spintharus? Among us you would be the Phrygian bird, the goldfinch, of the race of Philemon. Are you a slave and a Carian like Execestides?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Among us you can create yourself forefathers; you can always find relations. Does the son of Pisias want to betray the gates of the city to the foe? Let him become a partridge, the fitting offspring of his father; among us there is no shame in escaping as cleverly as a partridge.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Second Semi-Chorus: So the swans on the banks of the Hebrus ,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: tiotiotiotiotiotinx, mingle their voices to serenade Apollo, tiotiotiotinx, flapping their wings the while,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: tiotiotiotinx; their notes reach beyond the clouds of heaven; they startle the various tribes of the beasts; a windless sky calms the waves, totototototototototinx;
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: all Olympus resounds, and astonishment seizes its rulers; the Olympian graces and Muses cry aloud the strain, tiotiotiotinx.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of Second Semi-Chorus: There is nothing more useful nor more pleasant than to have wings. To begin with, just let us suppose a spectator to be dying with hunger and to be weary of the choruses of the tragic poets; if he were winged, he would fly off, go home to dine and come back with his stomach filled.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Some Patroclides, needing to take a crap, would not have to spill it out on his cloak, but could fly off, satisfy his requirements, let a few farts and, having recovered his breath, return. If one of you, it matters not who, had adulterous relations and saw the husband of his mistress in the seats of the senators,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: he might stretch his wings, fly to her, and, having laid her, resume his place. Is it not the most priceless gift of all, to be winged? Look at Diitrephes! His wings were only wicker-work ones, and yet he got himself chosen Phylarch and then Hipparch; from being nobody,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: he has risen to be famous; he's now the finest gilded cock of his tribe.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Halloa! What's this? By Zeus! I never saw anything so funny in all my life.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: What makes you laugh?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Your little wings. D'you know what you look like?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Like a goose painted by some dauber.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: And you look like a close-shaven blackbird.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: We ourselves asked for this transformation, and, as Aeschylus has it, These are no borrowed feathers, but truly our own.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Epops: Come now, what must be done?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: First give our city
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: a great and famous name, then sacrifice to the gods.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: I think so too.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: Let's see. What shall our city be called?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Will you have a high-sounding Laconian name? Shall we call it Sparta ?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: What!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: call my town Sparta ? Why, I would not use esparto for my bed, even though I had nothing but bands of rushes.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Well then, what name can you suggest?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Some name borrowed from the clouds, from these lofty regions in which we dwell —in short, some well-known name.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Do you like Nephelococcygia?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: Oh! capital!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: truly that's a brilliant thought!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Is it in Nephelococcygia that all the wealth of Theogenes and most of Aeschines' is?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: No, it's rather the plain of Phlegra, where the gods
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: withered the pride of the sons of the Earth with their shafts.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: Oh! what a splendid city! But what god shall be its patron? for whom shall we weave the peplus?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Why not choose Athena Polias?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Oh! what a well-ordered town it would be
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: to have a female deity armed from head to foot, while Clisthenes was spinning!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: Who then shall guard the Pelargicon?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: A bird
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Leader of the Chorus: One of us? What kind of bird?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: A bird of Persian strain, who is everywhere proclaimed to be the bravest of all,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: a true chick of Ares.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: Oh! noble chick!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Because he is a god well suited to live on the rocks. Come! into the air with you to help the workers who are building the wall; carry up rubble, strip yourself to mix the mortar,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: take up the hod, tumble down the ladder, if you like, post sentinels, keep the fire smouldering beneath the ashes, go round the walls, bell in hand, and go to sleep up there yourself; then despatch two heralds, one to the gods above, the other to mankind on earth
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: and come back here.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Euelpides: As for yourself, remain here, and may the plague take you for a troublesome fellow! He departs.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Go, friend, go where I send you, for without you my orders cannot be obeyed. For myself, I want to sacrifice to the new god, and I am going to summon the priest who must preside at the ceremony.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Slaves! slaves! bring forward the basket and the lustral water.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Chorus: I do as you do, and I wish as you wish, and I implore you to address powerful and solemn prayers to the gods, and in addition
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: to immolate a sheep as a token of our gratitude. Let us sing the Pythian chant in honor of the god, and let Chaeris accompany our voices.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Enough! but, by Heracles! what is this?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Great gods! I have seen many prodigious things, but I never saw a muzzled raven. The Priest arrives. Priest! it's high time! Sacrifice to the new gods.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Priest: I begin, but where is the man with the basket? Pray to the Hestia of the birds, to the kite, who presides over the hearth, and to all the god and goddess-birds who dwell in Olympus . . .
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Oh! Hawk, the sacred guardian of Sunium, oh, god of the storks!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Priest: . . . to the swan of Delos , to Leto the mother of the quails, and to Artemis, the goldfinch . . .
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: It's no longer Artemis Colaenis, but Artemis the goldfinch.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Priest: . . . to Bacchus, the finch and Cybele, the ostrich and mother of the gods and mankind. . .
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Oh! sovereign ostrich Cybele, mother of Cleocritus!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Priest: . . . to grant health and safety to the Nephelococcygians as well as to the dwellers in Chios . . .
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: The dwellers in Chios ! Ah! I am delighted they should be thus mentioned on all occasions.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Priest: . . . to the heroes, the birds, to the sons of heroes, to the porphyrion, the pelican, the spoon-bill, the redbreast, the grouse, the peacock, the horned-owl, the teal, the bittern, the heron, the stormy petrel, the fig-pecker, the titmouse . . .
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Stop! stop! you drive me crazy with your endless list. Why, wretch,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: to what sacred feast are you inviting the vultures and the sea-eagles? Don't you see that a single kite could easily carry off the lot at once? Begone, you and your fillets and all; I shall know how to complete the sacrifice by myself.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Chorus: It is imperative that I sing another sacred chant for the rite of the lustral water, and that I invoke
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: the immortals, or at least one of them, provided always that you have some suitable food to offer him; from what I see here, in the shape of gifts, there is naught whatever but horn and hair.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Let us address our sacrifices and our prayers to the winged gods.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Poet: Oh, Muse! celebrate happy Nephelococcygia in your hymns.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: What have we here? Where did you come from, tell me? Who are you?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Poet: I am he whose language is sweeter than honey, the zealous slave of the Muses,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: as Homer has it.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: You a slave! and yet you wear your hair long?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Poet: No, but the fact is all we poets are the assiduous slaves of the Muses, according to Homer.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: In truth your little cloak is quite holy too through zeal! But, poet, what ill wind drove you here?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Poet: I have composed verses in honor of your Nephelococcygia, a host of splendid dithyrambs and parthenia worthy of Simonides himself.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: And when did you compose them? How long since?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Poet: Oh! 'tis long, aye, very long, that I have sung in honor of this city.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: But I am only celebrating its foundation with this sacrifice; I have only just named it, as is done with little babies.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Poet: Just as the chargers fly with the speed of the wind, so does the voice of the Muses take its flight. Oh! thou noble founder of the town of Aetna thou, whose name recalls the holy sacrifices,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: make us such gift as thy generous heart shall suggest. He puts out his hand.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: He will drive us silly if we do not get rid of him by some present. To the Priest's acolyte. Here! you, who have a fur as well as your tunic, take it off and give it to this clever poet. Come,
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: take this fur; you look to me to be shivering with cold.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Poet: My Muse will gladly accept this gift; but engrave these verses of Pindar's on your mind.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Oh! what a pest! It's impossible then to get rid of him!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Poet: Straton wanders among the Scythian nomads, but has no linen garment. He is sad at only wearing an animal's pelt and no tunic.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Do you get what I mean?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: I understand that you want me to offer you a tunic. Hi! you To the acolyte. take off yours; we must help the poet. . . . Come, you, take it and get out.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Poet: I am going, and these are the verses that I address to this city:
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Phoebus of the golden throne, celebrate this shivery, freezing city; I have travelled through fruitful and snow-covered plains. Tralala! Tralala! He departs.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: What are you chanting us
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: about frosts? Thanks to the tunic, you no longer fear them. Ah! by Zeus! I could not have believed this cursed fellow could so soon have learnt the way to our city. To a slave. Come, take the lustral water and circle the altar. Let all keep silence!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Oracle-Monger: Let not the goat be sacrificed.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Who are you?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Oracle-Monger: Who am I? An oracle-monger.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Get out!
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Oracle-Monger: Wretched man, insult not sacred things. For there is an oracle of Bacis, which exactly applies to Nephelococcygia.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Why did you not reveal it to me before
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: I founded my city?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Oracle-Monger: The divine spirit was against it.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Well, I suppose there's nothing to do but hear the terms of the oracle.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Oracle-Monger: But when the wolves and the white crows shall dwell together between Corinth and Sicyon ...
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: But how do the Corinthians concern me?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Oracle-Monger: It is the regions of the air that Bacis indicates in this manner. They must first sacrifice a white-fleeced goat to Pandora, and give the prophet who first reveals my words a good cloak and new sandals.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Does it say sandals there?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Oracle-Monger: Look at the book.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: And besides this a goblet of wine and a good share of the entrails of the victim.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Of the entrails —does it say that?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Oracle-Monger: Look at the book. If you do as I command, divine youth, you shall be an eagle among the clouds; if not, you shall be neither turtle-dove, nor eagle, nor woodpecker.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Does it say all that?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Oracle-Monger: Look at the book.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: This oracle in no sort of way resembles the one Apollo dictated to me: If an impostor comes without invitation to annoy you during the sacrifice and to demand a share of the victim,

passages.text: apply a stout stick to his ribs.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Oracle-Monger: You are drivelling.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Look at the book. And don't spare him, were he an eagle from out of the clouds, were it Lampon himself or the great Diopithes.

passages.text: Oracle-Monger: Does it say that?

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Look at the book
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: and go and hang yourself.

passages.text: Oracle-Monger: Oh! unfortunate wretch that I am. He departs.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Away with you, and take your prophecies elsewhere.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Meton: I have come to you . . .
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: Yet another pest! What have you come to do? What's your plan? What's the purpose of your journey? Why these splendid buskins?
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: In the name of the gods, who are you?

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: What are these things?

passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: a square within this circle; in its center will be the market-place, into which all the straight streets will lead, converging to this center like a star, which, although only orbicular, sends forth its rays in a straight line from all sides.
passages.locusKind: TEI English line marker; segment not automatically aligned to Greek passage

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: A regular Thales!

passages.text: Pisthetaerus: I warned you.

passages.text: Now, be off, and do your surveying somewhere else.
